summary.text: Assume the primes of the form \(x^4+1\) are bounded by \(B\), and apply the positivity hypothesis at \(n=2B^2+B+3\); the resulting decomposition \(n=p+q\) gives \(x=\phi(p)\phi(q)\) with \(x^4+1\le B\), hence both totients are at most \(B\). Using \(\phi(p)=p-1\) and the general bound \(q\le 2\phi(q)^2\), one gets \(p\le B+1\) and \(q\le2B^2\), contradicting the chosen value of \(n=p+q\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(\varphi\) denote Euler’s totient function, with the usual extension \(\varphi(0)=0\). For \(n\in\mathbb N\), the number \(a(n)\) counts those integers \(p<n\) for which
\[
p\text{ is prime},\qquad q:=n-p>0,
\]
and
\[
\bigl(\varphi(p)\varphi(q)\bigr)^4+1
\]
is prime. Assume throughout that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every }n>2.
\]
We prove that there are infinitely many primes of the form \(x^4+1\).

We first establish the totient estimate that will provide the required growth contradiction.

**Totient estimate.** For every nonnegative integer \(r\),
\[
r\le 2\varphi(r)^2.
\tag{1}
\]
Moreover, if \(r\) is odd, then the stronger estimate
\[
r\le \varphi(r)^2
\tag{2}
\]
holds.

We prove both assertions simultaneously by strong induction on \(r\). They are immediate for \(r=0\) and \(r=1\). Now suppose \(r>1\), let \(s\) be the least prime factor of \(r\), and write
\[
r=sm,
\]
where \(m=r/s<r\). Thus the two inductive estimates are available for \(m\).

We use the following standard prime-factor identities for the totient. If \(s\) is prime and \(s\mid m\), then
\[
\varphi(sm)=s\varphi(m),
\tag{3}
\]
whereas if \(s\nmid m\), then
\[
\varphi(sm)=(s-1)\varphi(m).
\tag{4}
\]
The second identity follows from multiplicativity of \(\varphi\), since then \(s\) and \(m\) are coprime and \(\varphi(s)=s-1\). The first follows by increasing by one the exponent of \(s\) in the prime factorization of \(m\): this multiplies both the integer and its totient by \(s\).

First suppose that \(s\mid m\). By induction,
\[
m\le 2\varphi(m)^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
r=sm\le 2s\varphi(m)^2\le 2s^2\varphi(m)^2
   =2\bigl(s\varphi(m)\bigr)^2
   =2\varphi(r)^2,
\]
where we used \(s\ge1\) and (3). If \(r\) is odd, then both \(s\) and \(m\) are odd. The stronger inductive estimate for \(m\) therefore gives
\[
r=sm\le s\varphi(m)^2\le s^2\varphi(m)^2
  =\varphi(r)^2.
\]
This proves both desired estimates in this case.

Now suppose that \(s\nmid m\), so that (4) applies. There are two subcases for the general estimate (1). If \(s=2\), then \(2\nmid m\), so \(m\) is odd. We may therefore apply the stronger inductive estimate to \(m\), obtaining
\[
r=2m\le 2\varphi(m)^2
 =2\bigl((2-1)\varphi(m)\bigr)^2
 =2\varphi(r)^2.
\]
If \(s\ne2\), then the prime \(s\) satisfies \(s\ge3\). For every integer \(s\ge3\),
\[
s\le(s-1)^2:
\tag{5}
\]
indeed, writing \(k=s-1\ge2\), one has \(k+1\le k^2\). Using the general inductive estimate for \(m\), (5), and (4), we get
\[
r=sm\le 2s\varphi(m)^2
 \le 2(s-1)^2\varphi(m)^2
 =2\varphi(r)^2.
\]
Finally, if \(r\) is odd, then both factors \(s\) and \(m\) are odd. In particular \(s\ge3\), and the stronger inductive estimate for \(m\), followed by (5), gives
\[
r=sm\le s\varphi(m)^2
 \le (s-1)^2\varphi(m)^2
 =\varphi(r)^2.
\]
This completes the strong induction and proves (1) and (2).

We now prove the infinitude statement. Suppose, to the contrary, that the set
\[
\mathcal S=\{P\in\mathbb N: P\text{ is prime and }P=x^4+1
                  \text{ for some }x\in\mathbb N\}
\]
is finite. Any finite set of nonnegative integers is bounded, so choose \(B\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
P\le B\qquad\text{for every }P\in\mathcal S.
\tag{6}
\]
Set
\[
N=2B^2+B+3.
\]
Certainly \(N>2\), so the assumed positivity of \(a(N)\) supplies an integer \(p<N\) such that \(p\) is prime and, on putting
\[
q=N-p,
\]
the number
\[
\bigl(\varphi(p)\varphi(q)\bigr)^4+1
\tag{7}
\]
is prime. Since \(p<N\), we have \(q>0\), and \(N=p+q\).

Write
\[
x=\varphi(p)\varphi(q).
\]
The prime in (7) is \(x^4+1\), so it belongs to \(\mathcal S\). By (6),
\[
x^4+1\le B.
\tag{8}
\]
For every nonnegative integer \(x\), one has
\[
x\le x^4+1.
\]
This is clear for \(x=0\), while for \(x\ge1\), \(x=x^1\le x^4\). Thus (8) implies
\[
\varphi(p)\varphi(q)=x\le B.
\tag{9}
\]

Because \(q>0\), its totient is positive: \(\varphi(q)\ge1\). It follows from (9) that
\[
\varphi(p)\le B.
\tag{10}
\]
Since \(p\) is prime, \(\varphi(p)=p-1\). Hence (10) yields
\[
p\le B+1.
\tag{11}
\]
Also, a prime is at least \(2\), so \(\varphi(p)=p-1\ge1\). Reversing the two factors in (9) and using this positivity gives
\[
\varphi(q)\le B.
\tag{12}
\]
Applying the general totient estimate (1) to \(q\), and then (12), we obtain
\[
q\le2\varphi(q)^2\le2B^2.
\tag{13}
\]

Combining \(N=p+q\), (11), and (13), we find
\[
N\le (B+1)+2B^2=2B^2+B+1.
\tag{14}
\]
But by its definition,
\[
N=2B^2+B+3,
\]
which contradicts (14). Therefore \(\mathcal S\) cannot be finite. Hence there are infinitely many primes of the form \(x^4+1\), as claimed.
